label: Male puberty begins at about fourteen with seed and pubic hair
claim: In most cases a boy begins to produce seed at about fourteen years of age, and pubic hair appears at the same time.
quote: When twice seven years old, in the most of cases, the male begins to engender seed; and at the same time hair appears upon the pubes
measurable_quantities: age at onset of pubic hair (Tanner stage 2)
candidate_data: Pubertal timing cohorts and surveys such as NHANES and longitudinal growth studies reporting age at spermarche and pubic hair stages.

label: Menstruation and breast growth begin at about fourteen in girls
claim: In girls, at about fourteen years of age (the same age as male puberty), the breasts swell and menstruation begins.
quote: At the same age in the female, the breasts swell and the so-called catamenia commence to flow
candidate_data: Age-at-menarche data from NHANES, the Demographic and Health Surveys and historical menarche series.

label: Semen is infertile until twenty-one and young parents have small, imperfect offspring
claim: Until about the age of twenty-one a man's seed is infertile; after that it becomes fertile, but very young men and women produce undersized and imperfect offspring, as do young animals generally.
quote: At the outset and till the age of one and twenty the spermatic discharge is devoid of fecundity; afterwards it becomes fertile, but young men and women produce undersized and imperfect progeny, as is the case also with the common run of animals.
scope: humans, and animals generally for the effect of parental youth
measurable_quantities: birth weight and congenital anomaly rates by maternal and paternal age
candidate_data: National birth registries and vital statistics giving birth weight and anomalies by parental age; the Human Fertility Database for age-specific fertility.

label: Thick, granular semen tends to produce males and thin semen females
claim: Thin seed is infertile; granular seed is fertile and likely to produce male children, while thin, unclotted seed tends to produce female children.
quote: When the spermatic fluid is of a thin consistency it is infertile; when granular it is fertile and likely to produce male children, but when thin and unclotted it is apt to produce female offspring.
measurable_quantities: offspring sex ratio by semen consistency
candidate_data: Clinical semen-analysis datasets linked to IVF and pregnancy outcomes, including offspring sex; none known as a public standard resource.

label: In non-viviparous animals the menstrual residue becomes body, scales and feathers
claim: Animals that do not bear live young have no menstrual discharge, because the corresponding residue is turned into bodily substance, scutes, scales or feathers; in viviparous quadrupeds it becomes hair, flesh and urine, and only in women is it discharged.
quote: In creatures that do not bring forth their young alive nothing of the sort manifests itself, this particular superfluity being converted into bodily substance
scope: all animals; oviparous animals (birds, reptiles, fishes) contrasted with viviparous quadrupeds and women
measurable_quantities: presence or absence of menstruation across taxa
candidate_data: Comparative reproductive physiology surveys of menstruation across mammals; the Animal Diversity Web for reproductive traits.

label: A male foetus first moves at about forty days, a female at about ninety
claim: A male foetus usually first moves on the right side of the womb at about the fortieth day, a female on the left side at about the ninetieth day, though there are many exceptions.
quote: In the case of male children the first movement usually occurs on the right-hand side of the womb and about the fortieth day, but if the child be a female then on the left-hand side and about the ninetieth day.
measurable_quantities: gestational age at first foetal movement by sex
side of first movement by sex
candidate_data: Obstetric ultrasound studies of onset of foetal movement by sex; maternal quickening surveys.

label: An aborted male embryo at forty days is ant-sized with limbs and eyes visible
claim: A male human embryo aborted at the fortieth day is about the size of a large ant, with all the limbs, the penis and the disproportionately large eyes plainly visible.
quote: If the membrane be pulled to bits the embryo is revealed, as big as one of the large kind of ants; and all the limbs are plain to see, including the penis, and the eyes also, which as in other animals are of great size.
scope: human embryos at about forty days
measurable_quantities: crown-rump length at about six weeks
visibility of limbs, eyes and genital tubercle
candidate_data: Embryological staging collections such as the Carnegie stages and the Human Developmental Biology Resource.

label: Female embryos develop more slowly in the womb than male embryos
claim: In the womb a female embryo completes the development of its parts more slowly than a male, and more often than a male takes ten months to reach full term.
quote: In short, while within the womb, the female infant accomplishes the whole development of its parts more slowly than the male, and more frequently than the man-child takes ten months to come to perfection.
measurable_quantities: embryonic developmental stage by sex at fixed age
candidate_data: National birth registries giving gestational age by infant sex.

label: Humans alone have a variable term of pregnancy, from seven to eleven months
claim: Every other animal has a single fixed term of pregnancy, but in humans alone it varies, lasting seven, eight, nine or, most commonly, ten months, and occasionally into the eleventh.
quote: But in the case of mankind alone of all animals the times are diverse; for pregnancy may be of seven months' duration, or of eight months or of nine, and still more commonly of ten months, while some few women go even into the eleventh month.
scope: humans compared with all other animals
measurable_quantities: variance of gestation length in humans
variance of gestation length in other mammals
candidate_data: Human birth registries for gestational age; AnAge and the Amniote Life-History Database for gestation lengths in other mammals (variance would need primary studies).

label: Children born before seven months never survive
claim: Children born before the seventh month of pregnancy can never survive; seven-month children are the earliest viable, and most of them are weakly.
quote: Children that come into the world before seven months can under no circumstances survive. The seven-months' children are the earliest that are capable of life, and most of them are weakly
measurable_quantities: survival by gestational age at birth
candidate_data: Neonatal survival-by-gestational-age data from national birth and infant death registries; historical pre-incubator series would be needed for a fair test.

label: Eight-month children mostly die in Greece but survive in Egypt
claim: Children born in the eighth month are reared successfully in Egypt and some other places, but in Greece only a few survive and most perish.
quote: in these places the eight-months' children live and are brought up, but in Greece it is only a few of them that survive while most perish.
scope: human births at about eight months' gestation, Egypt versus Greece
candidate_data: Neonatal survival by gestational week from modern registries; ancient regional data none known.

label: The most children a woman has borne at one birth is five
claim: The largest number of children ever born to a woman at one birth is five, which has been observed several times.
quote: The largest number ever brought forth is five, and such an occurrence has been witnessed on several occasions.
candidate_data: Multiple-birth records from national vital statistics and medical case reports.

label: Women and mares, unlike other animals, accept the male during pregnancy
claim: Of all animals the woman and the mare are most inclined to accept mating during pregnancy; all other animals avoid the male when pregnant, except those that show superfoetation, such as the hare.
quote: Of all animals the woman and the mare are most inclined to receive the commerce of the male during pregnancy; while all other animals when they are pregnant avoid the male, save those in which the phenomenon of superfoetation occurs, such as the hare.
scope: humans, horses, hares and other animals
measurable_quantities: frequency of mating during pregnancy by species
candidate_data: Behavioural studies of mating during gestation in mammals; reproductive studies of superfetation in the European brown hare (Lepus europaeus).

label: Menstruation ceases at about forty, at the latest fifty, ending childbearing
claim: In most women menstruation ceases at about forty; in some it lasts until fifty, and women of that age have borne children, but none beyond it.
quote: the menstrual discharges ceases in most women about their fortieth year; but with those in whom it goes on longer it lasts even to the fiftieth year, and women of that age have been known to bear children. But beyond that age there is no case on record.
measurable_quantities: maximum maternal age at natural conception
candidate_data: Age-at-menopause cohort studies and the Human Fertility Database for age-specific fertility at 40–50+.

label: Men remain fertile to sixty and sometimes seventy
claim: Men in most cases remain sexually competent until sixty, and some until seventy; men have fathered children at seventy.
quote: Men in most cases continue to be sexually competent until they are sixty years old, and if that limit be overpassed then until seventy years; and men have been actually known to procreate children at seventy years of age.
candidate_data: Paternal-age distributions in national birth registries.

label: Children often inherit their parents' deformities and acquired marks
claim: Deformed parents produce deformed children (lame from lame, blind from blind), and children often inherit their parents' peculiarities, including marks such as pimples or scars.
quote: From deformed parents come deformed children, lame from lame and blind from blind, and, speaking generally, children often inherit anything that is peculiar in their parents and are born with similar marks, such as pimples or scars.
measurable_quantities: recurrence of parental congenital and acquired traits in offspring
candidate_data: Family recurrence data for congenital disorders (e.g. OMIM entries and registry studies); offspring of parents with acquired injuries as a control.

label: Resemblance can skip a generation and reappear in grandchildren
claim: Children usually resemble their parents or ancestors, but resemblance can be passed on after several generations, appearing in a grandchild but not in the child.
quote: While children mostly resemble their parents or their ancestors, it sometimes happens that no such resemblance is to be traced. But parents may pass on resemblance after several generations
measurable_quantities: frequency of traits reappearing in grandchildren but absent in parents
candidate_data: Pedigree data for recessive traits, e.g. OMIM and published family studies.

label: All animals develop in the same way, differing in where the navel attaches
claim: All animals, whether flying, swimming or walking, viviparous or oviparous, develop in the same way, except that in viviparous animals the navel is attached to the womb, in others to the egg, and in certain fishes to both.
quote: All animals whatsoever, whether they fly or swim or walk upon dry land, whether they bring forth their young alive or in the egg, develop in the same way: save only that some have the navel attached to the womb, namely the viviparous animals, and some have it attached to the egg, and some to both parts alike, as in a certain sort of fishes.
scope: all animals; 'a certain sort of fishes' (placental sharks such as the smooth dogfish)
measurable_quantities: umbilical attachment to uterus, yolk or both across taxa
candidate_data: Comparative embryology in the literature and Uberon/Phenoscape annotations of yolk-sac and placental structures.

label: All animals are born head first in the natural course
claim: All animals are at first head-upward in the womb but turn downward near term, and in the natural course birth in all animals is head first.
quote: birth in the natural course of things takes place in all animals head foremost
measurable_quantities: proportion of head-first presentations by species
candidate_data: Veterinary obstetric data on foetal presentation in horses, cattle and sheep; cetacean birth observations (often tail-first).

label: The navel-string has four vessels in oxen, two in smaller animals, one in fowls
claim: The navel-string contains four blood vessels in large animals such as oxen, two in smaller animals, and only one in very small ones such as fowls.
quote: In the larger animals, such as the embryos of oxen, the vessels are four in number, and in smaller animals two; in the very little ones, such as fowls, one vessel only.
measurable_quantities: number of umbilical vessels by species and body size
candidate_data: Comparative embryology and veterinary anatomy texts; Uberon annotations of umbilical artery and vein.

label: Children cut their first teeth in the seventh month, front teeth first
claim: Children begin cutting teeth in the seventh month, the front teeth first, upper or lower; teeth come sooner the warmer the nurse's milk.
quote: children begin to cut their teeth in the seventh month; and the front teeth are the first to come through, sometimes the upper and sometimes the lower ones.
candidate_data: Paediatric tooth-eruption norms from growth cohort studies.

label: Menstruation is suppressed while milk flows
claim: As a general rule menstruation does not occur while a woman is producing milk, because moisture is not directed in several directions at once.
quote: So long as there is a flow of milk the menstrual purgations do not take place, at least as a general rule, though the discharge has been known to occur during the period of suckling.
candidate_data: Demographic and Health Surveys data on postpartum amenorrhoea and breastfeeding duration.

label: Most animals show traces of the psychical qualities found in man
claim: Most animals show traces of psychical qualities such as gentleness, fierceness, courage, timidity and something like sagacity, which differ from man's either in degree or by analogy.
quote: In the great majority of animals there are traces of psychical qualities or attitudes, which qualities are more markedly differentiated in the case of human beings.
candidate_data: Animal personality and comparative cognition studies bear on it, but the claim is framed conceptually; none known as a single dataset.

label: Nature passes by degrees from lifeless things to animals with no sharp boundary
claim: Nature proceeds little by little from lifeless things through plants to animals, so that no exact boundary can be drawn and intermediate forms cannot be assigned to one side or the other.
quote: Nature proceeds little by little from things lifeless to animal life in such a way that it is impossible to determine the exact line of demarcation, nor on which side thereof an intermediate form should lie.
scope: all living and non-living things; intermediate forms such as sponges, ascidians, sea-anemones and sessile shellfish
candidate_data: none known

label: More intelligent animals with memory stay longer with their young
claim: Some animals simply breed at definite seasons, others also feed their young and then leave them, while the more intelligent animals with memory live with their offspring for longer and more socially.
quote: other animals are more intelligent and endowed with memory, and they live with their offspring for a longer period and on a more social footing.
measurable_quantities: relative brain size or cognitive measures
candidate_data: Parental-care trait compilations with brain-size data, e.g. the Amniote Life-History Database combined with published mammal and bird brain-mass datasets.

label: Air-breathing aquatic animals drown unless they surface to breathe
claim: Some air-breathing animals that live in water, such as the sea-turtle, crocodile, hippopotamus, seal, freshwater tortoise and frog, choke or drown unless they breathe air from time to time, and they breed on or near land.
quote: now all these animals choke or drown if they do not from time to time breathe atmospheric air: they breed and rear their young on dry land, or near the land, but they pass their lives in water.
scope: sea-turtle, crocodile, hippopotamus, seal, freshwater tortoise, frog
candidate_data: Life-history and respiration traits in AmphiBIO, the Animal Diversity Web and reptile trait compilations.

label: The dolphin breathes air with lungs and suffocates when caught in nets
claim: The dolphin breathes air into lungs, suffocates quickly when caught in nets, can live a considerable time out of water, and sleeps with its nose above water in order to breathe.
quote: he also inhales air into his lungs; for, by the way, the creature is furnished with this organ and respires thereby, and accordingly, when caught in the nets, he is quickly suffocated for lack of air.
scope: dolphins and other cetaceans with a blow-hole
candidate_data: Cetacean anatomy in Uberon/Phenoscape and bycatch mortality records in fisheries observer data.

label: Aquatic animals take in water to cool the blood, as land animals take in air
claim: Some aquatic animals take in water and discharge it for the same reason that air-breathers inhale air, to cool the blood; blooded animals that do this have gills, while those that take in water while catching prey have a blow-hole.
quote: some aquatic animals take in water and discharge it again, for the same reason that leads air-breathing animals to inhale air: in other words, with the object of cooling the blood.
measurable_quantities: function of gill ventilation (gas exchange versus heat exchange)
candidate_data: Comparative respiratory physiology literature on gill gas exchange and thermal exchange in fishes.

label: The cordylus (water-newt) has gills instead of lungs yet walks on land
claim: The cordylus or water-newt is the only known animal that takes in water through gills, having no lungs, yet is a four-footed animal that walks on land and gets its living there.
quote: this creature is furnished not with lungs but with gills, but for all that it is a quadruped and fitted for walking on dry land.
scope: cordylus (probably a larval or neotenic newt or salamander)
measurable_quantities: presence of gills and lungs in newt larvae and adults
candidate_data: AmphiBIO and the Animal Diversity Web for respiration and life stages of European newts.

label: A small change in a minute organ can change an animal's whole form
claim: A change in a minute organ can cause an immense change in an animal's overall form; castration, mutilating one small organ, turns a male towards the female form, and a slight change in size of an essential organ in the embryo decides whether it becomes male or female.
quote: The fact is that animals, if they be subjected to a modification in minute organs, are liable to immense modifications in their general configuration. This phenomenon may be observed in the case of gelded animals: only a minute organ of the animal is mutilated, and the creature passes from the male to the female form.
scope: animals generally; castrated males; embryonic sex determination
measurable_quantities: effect of early gonadal changes on sexual phenotype
candidate_data: Endocrinology and developmental-biology literature on castration and gonadal sex determination.

label: An empty wax vessel lowered into the sea fills with fresh water within a day
claim: Sea water contains fresh water that can be strained from it: an empty thin vessel of moulded wax let down into the sea will within twenty-four hours contain fresh, drinkable water.
quote: Take a thin vessel of moulded wax, attach a cord to it, and let it down quite empty into the sea: in twenty-four hours it will be found to contain a quantity of water, and the water will be fresh and drinkable.
scope: sea water; sessile testaceans said to feed on fresh water
measurable_quantities: salinity of water collected in a sealed wax vessel after 24 hours submersion
candidate_data: none known; would need a replication experiment.

label: All fishes eat their own species except the mullet
claim: All fishes eat members of their own species, with the single exception of the mullet; the conger is especially given to it.
quote: All fishes devour their own species, with the single exception of the cestreus or mullet; and the conger is especially ravenous in this respect.
measurable_quantities: occurrence of cannibalism in diet studies by species
candidate_data: Diet composition records in FishBase and published stomach-content studies.

label: Fishes have the stomach next to the mouth and no gullet
claim: Fishes have their stomachs close to the mouth and have no gullet, which is why some cast up their stomachs while chasing prey.
quote: fishes have their stomachs close to the mouth, and are not furnished with a gullet.
measurable_quantities: presence and length of oesophagus in fishes
candidate_data: Comparative fish anatomy in Uberon/Phenoscape (oesophagus annotations) and MorphoSource specimens.

label: The parrot-fish is the only fish that chews the cud
claim: Of all fishes the scarus (parrot-fish) is the only one known to chew the cud like a quadruped.
quote: Of all fishes the so-called scarus, or parrot, wrasse, is the only one known to chew the cud like a quadruped.
scope: Sparisoma cretense (Mediterranean parrotfish) versus other fishes
measurable_quantities: presence of regurgitation and re-chewing or pharyngeal grinding behaviour
candidate_data: Feeding-behaviour and pharyngeal-jaw studies of parrotfishes; FishBase species accounts.

label: Eels can live seven or eight years
claim: The eel lives in some cases for seven or eight years.
quote: The eel in some cases lives for seven or eight years.
candidate_data: Longevity records in AnAge and FishBase.

label: Birds with crooked talons are all carnivorous and cannot swallow grain
claim: Birds with crooked talons are carnivorous without exception and cannot swallow grain or bread even if it is put into their bills.
quote: Of birds, such as have crooked talons are carnivorous without exception, and cannot swallow corn or bread-food even if it be put into their bills in tit-bits
scope: raptors: eagles, kites, hawks, buzzard, lammergeier, vultures, owls
measurable_quantities: diet composition of raptors (proportion plant matter)
candidate_data: EltonTraits diet data and AVONET morphology for birds of prey.

label: Birds of prey almost never drink
claim: Birds as a rule drink very little, and birds of prey never drink at all apart from a very few that drink very rarely, such as the kestrel and the kite.
quote: In fact birds of prey never drink at all, excepting a very few, and these drink very rarely
measurable_quantities: water intake from prey versus free water
candidate_data: Avian water-balance physiology studies and field observations of raptor drinking.

label: Oviparous animals have a spongy, bloodless lung and drink little
claim: Scaly (tessellated) animals are spare drinkers, as are all animals with a spongy lung, and such a lung, poorly supplied with blood, is found in all oviparous animals.
quote: Tessellated animals are spare drinkers, as are also all such animals as have a spongy lung, and such a lung, scantily supplied with blood, is found in all oviparous animals.
scope: reptiles (lizards, snakes, tortoises) and other oviparous animals
candidate_data: Comparative lung morphology literature and Uberon/Phenoscape annotations; reptile water-balance studies.

label: Carnivores eat grass only when sick, to purge themselves
claim: Fierce, jag-toothed viviparous quadrupeds are all carnivorous and never eat grass except when sick, as dogs eat grass to make themselves vomit.
quote: These carnivorous animals never eat grass except when they are sick, just as dogs bring on a vomit by eating grass and thereby purge themselves.
measurable_quantities: frequency of grass-eating in healthy versus sick dogs
candidate_data: Veterinary surveys of plant-eating in dogs and cats.

label: A pig's carcass weighs five-sixths of its live weight
claim: A pig fattens faster for its size than any other animal, and after slaughter its flesh weighs five-sixths of its live weight, the hair, blood and the rest making up the other sixth.
quote: If a pig be weighed when living, you may calculate that after death its flesh will weigh five-sixths of that weight, and the hair, the blood, and the rest will weigh the other sixth.
candidate_data: Agricultural carcass-yield statistics for pigs (FAO and national livestock statistics).

label: Camels live about thirty years and occasionally to a hundred
claim: Camels live for about thirty years; some live much longer, and some have been known to reach a hundred.
quote: Camels live for about thirty years; in some exceptional cases they live much longer, and instances have been known of their living to the age of a hundred.
candidate_data: Longevity records in AnAge and PanTHERIA.

label: The bee is the only insect that always avoids rotten food
claim: The bee is the only insect that invariably avoids anything rotten and touches no food without a sweet juice.
quote: The bee is the only insect that invariably eschews whatever is rotten
scope: honey bee compared with other insects
measurable_quantities: acceptance of decaying food by honey bees and other insects
candidate_data: Honey bee foraging studies and insect feeding-guild records.

label: Cranes migrate from Scythia to the marshes at the source of the Nile
claim: Cranes migrate from the steppes of Scythia to the marshlands south of Egypt where the Nile rises.
quote: for these birds migrate from the steppes of Scythia to the marshlands south of Egypt where the Nile has its source.
candidate_data: GBIF occurrence data, Movebank tracking data and eBird for common crane migration.

label: Migrants are fatter leaving cold for warm lands than on the return
claim: All animals are fatter when migrating from cold to warm regions than when migrating from warm to cold; the quail is fatter when it leaves in autumn than when it arrives in spring.
quote: All creatures are fatter in migrating from cold to heat than in migrating from heat to cold; thus the quail is fatter when he emigrates in autumn than when he arrives in spring.
scope: migratory animals, especially the common quail
measurable_quantities: body mass or fat score of migrants in autumn versus spring
candidate_data: Bird-ringing body-mass and fat-score records from European ringing schemes and stopover studies.

label: Birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued and mimics
claim: As a general rule all birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued and given to mimicry, as is the parrot.
quote: As a general rule all birds with crooked talons are short-necked, flat-tongued, and disposed to mimicry.
scope: birds with hooked claws, including parrots and owls
candidate_data: AVONET morphology and published vocal-mimicry surveys across bird families.

label: The trichia leaves the Black Sea up the Danube into the Adriatic
claim: The trichia is caught entering but never leaving the Black Sea because it alone swims north into the Danube and, where the river divides, down into the Adriatic.
quote: The way of accounting for this phenomenon is that this fish, and this one only, swims northwards into the Danube, and then at the point of its bifurcation swims down southwards into the Adriatic.
scope: trichia (probably a sardine or shad) in the Black Sea, Danube and Adriatic
measurable_quantities: migration routes of clupeids between the Black Sea and Adriatic
hydrographic connection of the Danube to the Adriatic
candidate_data: Hydrography of the Danube basin and clupeid distribution and migration records in FishBase and GBIF.

label: Animals hide away against extreme heat as well as extreme cold
claim: Animals go into concealment (dormancy) as a refuge against extreme heat as well as extreme cold; shellfish all do so, snails in winter and the purple murex and scallop in the hottest season.
quote: animals go into concealment by way of refuge against extreme heat, as well as against extreme cold.
scope: animals generally; land snails, purple murex, scallop
measurable_quantities: occurrence of hibernation and aestivation by species and season
candidate_data: Published records of aestivation and hibernation in molluscs and other animals; AnAge notes on dormancy.

label: Snakes and lizards hide for four months in winter and eat nothing
claim: Scaly animals such as the serpent, lizard, gecko and river crocodile go into hiding for four months in the depth of winter and eat nothing during that time.
quote: all of which go into hiding for four months in the depth of winter, and during that time eat nothing.
candidate_data: Reptile brumation studies and life-history compilations for Mediterranean snakes and lizards and the Nile crocodile.

label: Many birds hide in winter rather than migrate, including swallows
claim: Many birds do not migrate to warmer countries but hide where they are in winter; swallows have often been found in holes without feathers, and the kite, stork, turtle-dove, lark and others go into hiding.
quote: A great number of birds also go into hiding; they do not all migrate, as is generally supposed, to warmer countries.
scope: swallow, kite, stork, owzel, turtle-dove, lark, thrush, starling, owl
measurable_quantities: winter presence or absence and torpor in these species
candidate_data: GBIF and eBird winter occurrence records, Movebank tracking of swallows and storks, and studies of avian torpor.

label: The she-bear gives birth during winter concealment and emerges in spring
claim: The she-bear gives birth while in winter concealment and stays hidden until she brings the cubs out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice; bears eat nothing while hidden.
quote: The female brings forth her young at this time, and remains in concealment until it is time to bring the cubs out; and she brings them out in spring, about three months after the winter solstice.
measurable_quantities: timing of birth relative to denning
candidate_data: Brown bear denning and reproduction studies; AnAge and PanTHERIA for reproductive timing.

label: Crustaceans moult not once but repeatedly
claim: Crabs, crawfish and lobsters slough their shells, becoming soft all over, and they do so not once for all but over and over again.
quote: These animals also do not cast their skins once and for all, but over and over again.
candidate_data: Crustacean growth and moult studies; SeaLifeBase species accounts.

label: Fishes have no pestilential diseases like those of man and livestock
claim: No pestilential (epidemic) disease is known to attack fishes as such diseases attack man, horses and oxen, although individual fishes do appear to fall sick.
quote: We know of no pestilential malady attacking fishes, such as those which attack man, and horses and oxen among the quadrupedal vivipara
measurable_quantities: occurrence of epizootic mass mortality in wild fish
candidate_data: WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health) aquatic animal disease reports and the literature on wild fish epizootics.

label: The purple murex dies within a day of tasting fresh water
claim: Shellfish generally benefit from rain, but the purple murex is an exception: placed near a river mouth, it dies within a day of tasting fresh water.
quote: if it be placed on a shore near to where a river discharges, it will die within a day after tasting the fresh water.
candidate_data: Salinity-tolerance experiments on Mediterranean murex snails; SeaLifeBase habitat data.

label: The pig is the only animal known to get measles
claim: The pig is the only animal known to suffer from 'measles' (pimples in the flesh, seen especially under the tongue), and pigs never get it while still sucklings.
quote: The pig is the only animal known to be subject to measles.
scope: pigs; 'measles' corresponds to cysticercosis (Taenia solium cysts)
candidate_data: Parasite host records for Taenia solium and other cysticerci in veterinary parasitology literature and the NHM host-parasite database.

label: Rabies passes to every animal bitten by a mad dog except man
claim: Rabies drives dogs mad and is fatal to them, and any animal bitten by a rabid dog catches it and dies, with the exception of man.
quote: ary animal whatever, excepting man, will take the disease if bitten by a dog so afflicted; the disease is fatal to the dog itself, and to any animal it may bite, man excepted.
measurable_quantities: transmission and fatality of rabies in humans versus other animals
candidate_data: WHO rabies surveillance and WOAH WAHIS animal rabies data.

label: The ass tolerates cold least and is absent from Scythia
claim: Of all animals of its kind the ass is least able to endure extreme cold, which is why it is not found on the shores of the Black Sea or in Scythia.
quote: Of all animals on its of its kind it is the least capable of enduring extreme cold, which circumstance will account for the fact that the animal is not found on the shores of the Euxine, nor in Scythia.
scope: donkey compared with horse and mule
measurable_quantities: historical distribution of donkeys in cold regions
candidate_data: Livestock census data (FAOSTAT) for donkey distribution by climate and physiological studies of donkey cold tolerance.

label: All insects die when smeared with oil
claim: All insects without exception die if smeared with oil, and die faster if the head is smeared and they are laid in the sun.
quote: All insects, without exception, die if they be smeared over with oil; and they die all the more rapidly if you smear their head with the oil and lay them out in the sun.
measurable_quantities: time to death by application site
candidate_data: Entomological studies of horticultural and mineral oil toxicity to insects.

label: The leopard is absent from Europe while lions live in part of Greece
claim: Lions are more numerous in Libya and in the part of Europe between the Achelous and the Nessus rivers; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor and is not found in Europe at all.
quote: lions are more numerous in Libya, and in that district of Europe that lies between the Achelous and the Nessus; the leopard is more abundant in Asia Minor, and is not found in Europe at all.
scope: lion and leopard in the ancient Mediterranean
measurable_quantities: historical and archaeozoological occurrence of lions and leopards in Greece and Europe
candidate_data: Archaeozoological records and fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database and GBIF.

label: Different species breed together if similar in size and gestation length
claim: In Libya animals of different species meet at watering places and pair, and such pairs often breed if they are nearly the same size and have gestation periods of the same length.
quote: such pairs will often breed if they be nearly of the same size and have periods of gestation of the same length.
measurable_quantities: hybrid fertility versus body-size and gestation-length differences between parent species
candidate_data: Mammalian hybrid compilations combined with body mass and gestation data from PanTHERIA and AnAge.

label: Wolves and dogs interbreed, and the Laconian hound is a fox–dog cross
claim: Animals of different kinds produce hybrids: in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch couple and breed, and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
quote: Elsewhere also bastard-animals are born to heterogeneous pairs; thus in Cyrene the wolf and the bitch will couple and breed; and the Laconian hound is a cross between the fox and the dog.
measurable_quantities: occurrence of wolf–dog and fox–dog hybrids
candidate_data: Canid genomic hybridization studies and records of wolf–dog admixture; reports on claimed fox–dog hybrids.

label: A scaly fish's age can be told from the size and hardness of its scales
claim: The age of a scaly fish can be told from the size and hardness of its scales.
quote: The age of a scaly fish may be told by the size and the hardness of its scales.
measurable_quantities: scale size and hardness versus known age
candidate_data: Fisheries scale-ageing (scalimetry) validation studies.
